title: Static Electricity
summary: How objects become charged by friction, how charges attract and repel, lightning and earthing, and everyday uses and dangers of static electricity.

notes.text: Atoms contain positive **protons** and negative **electrons**. A neutral object has equal numbers of each. Only **electrons** can move from one object to another; protons stay in the nucleus.

items: An object that **gains** electrons becomes **negatively** charged.
An object that **loses** electrons becomes **positively** charged.
Charge that builds up and stays on an object is called **static electricity** (static means not moving).

notes.title: Finding the charge
notes.problem: An atom has 11 protons and 11 electrons, then loses one electron. What is its charge now?
steps: Each proton is +1 and each electron is −1.
At first: +11 and −11 balance, so the atom is neutral.
notes.answer: The atom now has a charge of +1.

notes.text: When two different insulating materials are rubbed together, electrons are transferred from one to the other. Both objects end up with **equal but opposite** charges.

notes.title: Rubbing a plastic ruler with a woollen cloth
notes.problem: A plastic ruler is rubbed with a woollen cloth and becomes negatively charged. Explain what happened and state the charge on the cloth.
steps: Friction transferred electrons from the wool to the plastic.
The ruler gained electrons, so it is negatively charged.
The cloth lost the same number of electrons, so it is positively charged.
notes.answer: Electrons moved from the cloth to the ruler; the cloth is positive.

notes.label: Remember
notes.text: **Like charges repel, unlike charges attract.** A charged object can also attract small neutral objects such as pieces of paper, because it pulls the opposite charges in the paper slightly towards it.

Static electricity builds up on **insulators** (plastic, rubber, glass, wool), because charges cannot move through them. On a **conductor** (metal), the charge flows away, especially if the conductor is connected to the ground.
When static charge suddenly flows away, often as a spark, for example the small shock you feel after walking on a carpet and touching a metal door handle.

In a thunderstorm, water droplets and ice crystals rub together inside clouds. The bottom of the cloud becomes negatively charged. When the charge is large enough, a huge spark jumps between the cloud and the ground: **lightning**. Lightning heats the air so quickly that it expands explosively, producing **thunder**.

items: **Lightning conductors**: metal rods on tall buildings connected by a thick copper strip to the ground, so lightning flows safely into the earth.
In a storm, stay indoors or in a car, away from tall trees, water, open fields and metal fences.
If caught outdoors, crouch low with your feet together. Do not lie flat.

notes.text: Uses and dangers of static electricity

rows: Photocopiers and laser printers attract toner powder to paper
Sparks can ignite petrol vapour when refuelling cars or aircraft
Spray painting cars: charged paint droplets are attracted evenly to the car body
Electrostatic filters remove smoke and dust from factory chimneys

notes.text: **Earthing** prevents dangerous build-up: fuel tankers are connected to the ground with a wire before unloading, so any charge flows safely away.

questions.prompt: Explain how a lightning conductor protects a building.
questions.memo:
✓ It is a metal rod connected to the ground by a thick conducting strip (1)
✓ It provides an easy path for the charge to flow safely into the ground instead of through the building (1)

questions.prompt: A glass rod is rubbed with a silk cloth and becomes positively charged. Explain what happened to the electrons and state the charge on the silk.
questions.memo:
✓ Electrons were transferred from the glass rod to the silk by friction (1)
✓ The rod lost electrons, so it is positive (1)
✓ The silk gained electrons, so it is negatively charged (1)

questions.prompt: Why are fuel tankers earthed with a wire before petrol is pumped out?
questions.memo:
✓ Friction of the flowing fuel can build up static charge (1)
✓ A spark could ignite the petrol vapour; earthing lets the charge flow safely away (1)
